## Chapter 40: Process Maps

### Why Create Process Maps

Process maps aren't just simple flowcharts, although teams can choose to create a flowchart as the process map for a specific project or phase. Process maps are visual representations of a process and generally include every activity and decision within it. They can show various levels of the process, and we'll look in this chapter at the difference between high-level organizational process maps and detailed process maps.

Teams create process maps for several reasons. First, a process map is a good starting point when teams are trying to understand the overall process. If a visual representation of the process doesn't already exist, the team can work with subject-matter experts to create one. The act of creating the map is valuable in itself, because it lets the team ask many questions about the process and explore it deeply, in order to convert the knowledge gained into a functional diagram.

During the Measure phase, process maps can help teams understand which inputs or outputs should be measured, and when and where, during a process, data can or should be acquired. Process maps are also useful during the Analyze phase, because visual representations of a process's flow generally make it easier to see where rework happens or where bottlenecks might exist.

Process maps also let the team visualize a future state for a process. A Six Sigma team might start with a current-state process map during a project's Define phase and create a desired-state map during the Analyze or Improve phase. Side-by-side comparisons of the current-state and future-state maps let teams see exactly what changes need to be made, make sure every bit of current-state functionality is addressed in the updated process, and double-check that every challenge is resolved by the new process. Process maps can also help teams see whether they might be creating new challenges, like rework loops or bottlenecks, within an updated process.

Finally, process maps, in their various forms, are valuable documentation for a Six Sigma team and for an organization as a whole. Six Sigma teams can use all or part of the process maps they create in tollgate and other presentations, to make sure decision-makers, sponsors, and supporting staff understand the process before moving forward with any aspect of the project or making decisions about the project or process. Organizations can use process maps in training documents, or as a guide for non-Six Sigma employees who need to understand new processes or changes to existing processes.

### Two Types of Process Map

This chapter will cover two basic types of process map. The first is the flow chart, which presents a view of the process that typically flows from top to bottom on the page. Flow charts generally give the overview of a process or detail a specific part of the process. When multiple flow charts are used for detailed parts of a process, they can reference each other to provide a complete description of a process.

The second type of process map covered in this chapter is the swimlane process map, which generally provides a left-to-right and top-to-bottom view of the process. A swimlane process map divides the process into different sections, often by who's responsible for the work, when the work happens, or what type of work is being done. Teams can quickly see not just the flow of work through the process, but who or what is responsible for each step.

### Process Map Symbols

Many people try to create process maps using various shapes, connecting them with arrows to show the flow of work. That's the basic idea behind a flowchart or process map, but each shape type actually says something specific about the information presented within or near it. Anyone familiar with process map symbology should be able to look at a process map and discern various details just from the shapes and how they're presented. In this section, we'll cover most of the common flowchart/process map shapes and what they're used for.

**Process Shape**

The process shape is the most common shape in most process maps or flowcharts. It's a rectangle. Depending on how you plan to use the process map and what your company's design specifications are, you can use your Word, Excel, or Visio program's default colors, update the shape colors to match your company's branding or publication requirements, or create a simple black-and-white rectangle. This is true for every shape in this chapter.

A process shape is used to indicate an action step within the process. Something is happening, and it's generally a person, or people, carrying out the action. The description of the action is usually typed as text inside the shape, which also holds true for most of the shapes presented in this section.

**Alternate Process Shape**

The alternate process shape is used to indicate that an action is an alternative to something that's normal within the process. It's a rectangle with rounded corners.

**Predefined Process Shape**

A predefined process shape is used when there's a process within a process, and that subprocess is already defined in another document. The shape tells readers that more than one step is happening at that point in the overall process, and that those steps are formally documented somewhere else in the organization. The documentation might be in standard operating procedures, but it could also be in the form of another process map.

If a subprocess is known and a Six Sigma team decides not to fully document those steps — but the process isn't formally documented elsewhere, or the team doesn't know whether it is — then this shape shouldn't be used.

**Terminator Shape**

When looking at a map of a complex process, it can be hard to tell where the process starts and ends. This is especially true when a printed process map spans several pages and may have more than one possible endpoint. The terminator shape is used to show the start and end of a process. At the start, the terminator shape generally includes an action that triggers the rest of the process.

**Preparation Shape**

The preparation shape, which is a hexagon, indicates that a step in the process is preparation for something else. An example might be cleaning a piece of equipment before using it, or setting the oven temperature before preparing a recipe.

**Manual Operation Shape**

The manual operation shape indicates a part of the process that's carried out by a person and isn't automated. In processes that are mostly people-driven, you don't necessarily need to differentiate between manual operation steps and regular process steps. The manual operation step shape is actually more important to use when representing mostly automated or computerized processes, because you'd want the sudden need for human interaction within the process to stand out.

**Delay Shape**

The delay shape lets you indicate that a waiting period occurs in the process. Delay shapes can be valuable for Six Sigma teams, because they often indicate a possible point where muda is occurring. When teams see delay shapes on process maps, they should ask questions about why the delay is happening — is it, for example, because one process step is batching up outputs, and the next step is waiting for a batch? Is it because a bottleneck is occurring upstream in the process? These are valuable insights for a Six Sigma team.

**Decision Shape**

The decision shape indicates that a decision is being made in the process. Typically, the decision indicated by the diamond shape is a yes/no or go/no-go type. An example of this kind of decision branch in a process is seen when additional approval is needed for certain types of action. For example, a team that processes customer refunds might have some leeway to process smaller-value refunds without approvals. If the refund is less than $50, the team's request is processed with no additional action; if the refund is more than $50, it may need to involve a supervisor.

**Connector Shape**

A connector shape generally indicates a jump from one part of the process to another. Sometimes this shape is used to indicate that an audit or inspection happens at a certain part of the process.

**Document Shape**

The document shape indicates that a step in a process creates a document. Using the refund example above, at some point in that process, a check is printed. A check is a document, and that process step could use this shape.

**Multi-Document Shape**

The multi-document shape indicates a process step that creates multiple documents. Using the same refund example, it's possible the accounting department batches the checks, printing every refund at once, once a day or week. That process step could use this shape.

**Display Shape**

The display shape is used to show that a step in a process involves displaying some information to a person. For example, a person using a company communication portal to send an email might have to log into the portal first. During that process, the software might display a terms-of-use agreement; if the process of using the software were mapped, this shape could be used to indicate that step.

**Data Shape**

The data shape is used to show that inputs are entering a process, or that outputs are leaving a process. It's also called an Input/Output (I/O) shape.

**Manual Input Shape**

The manual input shape is used to show a step that involves a person manually typing in information, usually using a computer.

**Off-Page Connector Shape**

The off-page connector shape is used to show that part of the process is represented on another page. You can also use off-page connectors to link multiple processes documented across several pages.

**Or Shape**

The "or" shape is different from the basic diamond decision shape described earlier in this list. The "or" shape also indicates a branch in the process, generally in more than two possible directions. Typically, the process map provides some data on how to decide which branch the flow should follow at the "or" shape. For example, consider the refund example used above.

In the earlier scenario, there were two options for each refund request: either the request was less than $50 and could be processed, or it was more than $50 and had to be handled by a supervisor. In a new version of the process, work might follow one of three paths. First, if the refund request is $20 or less, it's automatically approved once entered by an employee and is routed to check generation. If the refund request is $20 to $50, it must be reviewed by a second employee, who has to agree with the refund decision before it's routed to the check process. If the refund is above $50, it must be approved by a supervisor before a check is issued.

On a process map, the three-branch decision would come out of the "or" shape. The instructions on which path to choose could be as simple as "Refund ≤ $20," "Refund $20 to $50," and "Refund > $50."

**Merge Shape**

If processes can branch based on decision shapes and "or" shapes, they can also come back together. When multiple workflow branches within a process come back together, you can indicate this with a merge shape.

**Extract Shape**

If processes split into two or more parallel flows with no decision or criteria involved, you can use an extract shape to indicate that fact. This isn't one of the more common symbols seen on process maps, and sometimes the triangle indicates something else. When the triangle is presented with an M inside it, it can indicate that a measurement should happen at that point in the workflow.

**Collate Data Shape**

The collate data shape is used when data or materials in a process need to be organized using a standard format. Cutting fabric to certain lengths before sewing, or sorting admission forms before considering them, are examples of when this symbol might be used.

**Sort Data Shape**

The sort data shape indicates that information or materials should be arranged in a certain order. Sorting materials by color before moving on to the next step in a manufacturing process could justify this symbol, for example.

Every shape within your flowchart or process map is connected by lines and arrows. Arrows matter, because they guide the reader through the map in the correct sequence.

### Where Do These Shapes Come From?

Every shape listed in this chapter is available in Microsoft programs, including Word, Excel, and Visio. For anyone without dedicated process-mapping software, Excel is probably one of the easiest programs to use for creating process maps and flowcharts. Just turn off the gridline display, to get a clean screen to work with.

You can insert every flowchart shape in Excel using the Insert → Shapes option.

**Beyond Word/Excel/Visio: dedicated BPMN tools.** For more formal process maps — especially when the process needs to be shared as a standardized, versioned model, or eventually simulated — it's worth considering a dedicated **BPMN 2.0** (Business Process Model and Notation) modeling tool, the international standard notation for business process maps. **Bizagi Modeler** is a widely used free option in this space: drag-and-drop interface, strict BPMN 2.0 compliance, documentation export to Word/PDF/Web, and cloud collaboration — with no coding required. The limitation, compared to more complete suites, is that advanced simulation and analytics features are more limited. For most of the Six Sigma process maps described in this chapter, the basic symbols (process, decision, terminator) are already enough in either tool — the choice between Excel/Visio and a dedicated BPMN tool is more a question of formality and model reuse than technical capability.

### Include a Legend with Your Process Map

Although someone familiar with process-mapping tools will recognize most of the symbols above quickly, not everyone in a business setting will. Most people in business settings are familiar with the basic process shape, the decision and connector shapes, and the terminator shape. Because of that, you can build most of most process maps using just those shapes. If you feel another shape is warranted, it's a good idea to add a process map legend to your diagram, to make sure anyone viewing it can follow along.

It's also a good idea to add a process map legend because not everyone uses every symbol above for exactly the same reasons. The connector shape can mean several different things, as can several of the other shapes.

You've probably noticed, reading through the list of common shapes, that some activities could fit two or even three process shapes. Outside a few basic rules, there's no strictly right or wrong way to add detail to a process map. In the end, the goal when creating a process map should be clarity. If adding a different type of shape will make the process easier to understand visually, then do it. If you can simply use the basic process shape along with text to explain the process, remember that, in Six Sigma, less really is more.

### Basic Flowcharts

<img alt="Basic flowchart: Start (oval terminator) → Input (parallelogram) → decision (diamond) branching into two Process boxes (rectangles) → End (oval terminator)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:395px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


A basic flowchart starts with a trigger activity, includes inputs and processes, decisions, and a final action. Flowcharts generally start at the top of the page and flow downward. Secondarily, you'd read a flowchart left to right as you move down the page, if a secondary direction is needed. In the flowchart above, you can see a trigger activity happens, which involves some kind of data entry. Using that input, a person makes a decision. That decision routes the workflow to the process on the right or the process on the left. After that action is completed, the overall process, as logged in this flowchart, ends.

It's important to note that the terminator ending the process mapped in the flowchart or process map rarely ends the work itself. The only time the final terminator signals the complete end of the work is when you're mapping the last process before the end customer, or you're mapping the whole company's process at a very high level. In most cases, though, the final terminator on your process map likely indicates the end of that specific process and the start of the next one. For example, at a beverage bottling plant, a team might be mapping the process that prepares bottles to receive ingredients. The process map starts when a new, clean bottle is introduced into the process, and ends when the bottle is clean, has a label, and is placed on the line to receive the liquid it'll hold. After the mapped process, the bottle goes through other processes to be filled, capped, inspected, and packaged.

### Creating a Swimlane Diagram

One of the most widely used process map formats in the Six Sigma world is the swimlane diagram. The swimlane diagram is a flowchart, but it's a flowchart that's somewhat bounded by lines and columns, known as swimlanes. You can draw your lanes in whatever way best represents the process you're working with. Two common options are:

1. Use columns to represent time or phases of activity in the process, and use rows to represent the person, department, or group responsible.
2. Use columns to represent the person, department, or group responsible, and use rows to represent time or phases of activity in the process.

<img alt="Generic swimlane diagram "Process name": columns for "Preparation phase", "Execution phase", and "Final phase", rows for "Department 1", "Department 2", and "Department 3", with process, decision, and terminator shapes distributed across the grid" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:620px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


No matter which method you choose, someone should be able to read your swimlane diagram starting in the top-left corner and reading right and down.

<img alt="Note on BPMN/Bizagi notation" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

<img alt="Bizagi Modeler-style swimlane diagram of the reimbursement approval process" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

### Start by Identifying the Lanes

Start your process map session by identifying the lanes associated with the process you're planning to map. If you've already done a SIPOC as part of a project's Define phase, you can use the information from that activity to build your lanes. If not, you can use some of the previous chapter's brainstorming activities to help generate ideas for your process map. Responsibility charts, for example, can help you understand how activities within the process might be divided into organic categories.

If you don't yet have a basic sense of possible lanes, first ask yourself or your team: what are all the process's steps? Don't worry yet about putting the steps in order, or even having every detailed step generated through brainstorming. You can add to your map as you build it. Since you don't want the team to start worrying too much about step order or how the steps connect, use index cards to write down the steps at this stage. Once the team feels every main step is jotted down, you can organize the steps into groups, to get a better sense of possible lanes.

To understand what lanes might look like in a real-world process, consider the process a brand uses to generate blog post ideas, write blog posts, and publish posts on a website. You can see, just from that previous sentence, that the process is already somewhat divided into main categories:

- Ideas are created
- Blog posts are written
- Blog posts are published

These three sections can become the row designations for the swimlane process map.

Now, consider that different people or groups handle each of the subcategories within the process. The marketing team generates the content ideas, a team of contract writers writes the blog posts, and an internal quality team reviews and then publishes the blogs.

The basis of the swimlane diagram might look like the figure below.

<img alt="Swimlane diagram base: three columns (Marketing Team, Contracted Writers, Quality Editors) and three rows (Idea creation, Blog writing, Blog posting), still empty" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### Create a Step-by-Step List of Process Activities

Next, create a simple, step-by-step list of every activity within the process. If you're familiar with a process and are creating a process map on your own, you can start placing the steps into shapes on the grid — you can always move them later as needed. If you're not familiar with the process, or you're working with a group to build the process map, it helps to gather the data first.

For the blog-generation example's purposes, here are a few steps included in the process.

1. At the start of each month, the marketing team generates ideas for next month's content.
2. The marketing team generates 15 to 25 ideas, but chooses only 8 to 10 ideas to be written.
3. Once the 8 to 10 items are chosen, the marketing team picks a title and keywords for each blog post.
4. The topic, along with any special instructions needed, the titles, and the keywords, are provided to the contract writing team.
5. The writers draft the blog posts.
6. The writers check whether the blog posts meet the guidelines.
7. The writers submit the blog posts.
8. The quality editors review the blog posts.
9. The quality editors check whether the blog posts meet the guidelines, and request revisions if they don't.
10. The quality editors do a line edit of the blog posts.
11. The quality editors format the blog posts.
12. The quality editors enter the posts into the blog platform.
13. The quality editors schedule the blog posts for publication the following month.

You can split the steps above across several lanes and rows. Steps 1 through 4 belong to the marketing team and, mostly, to the idea-creation row. The last step starts crossing rows into the process's next phase.

Steps 5 through 7 belong to the writing team and typically fit the process's writing phase. The last steps belong to the quality editor section, but involve a decision step that can send the work back to the writers.

Consider how steps 1 through 4 might be positioned on the swimlane diagram.

<img alt="Swimlane diagram with the "Marketing Team" column filled in: "Team lists new ideas for next month's blog" (terminator) → "Team chooses 8 to 10 ideas from those brainstormed" → "Keywords are chosen for each idea" (predefined process) → "Titles are chosen for each idea" → "Blog posts are assigned to writers" (crossing into the writers' lane)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:556px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The terminal shape — the activity that kicks off the whole process — is that the time has come to brainstorm blog ideas for the following month. The team brainstorms ideas and then chooses 8 to 10. For the next step, the activity is a predefined process. This means, somewhere, the company has a published SOP or guidelines for researching and applying keywords to blog post ideas. Once that's done, someone picks a title for each idea, and the blogs are assigned to writers. Notice that the final activity — assigning the blogs to writers — sits in a rectangle that partly crosses the lane line. That's a useful visual cue that responsibility for the work, at that point in the process, shifts from the marketing team to the writers.

Next, consider how steps 5 and 7 might look on the process map.

<img alt="Swimlane diagram showing the transition into the "Contracted Writers" column: "Blog posts are assigned to writers" crossing over from Marketing → "Blog is written" → "Blog checked against guidelines and edited" → "Blog submitted" (crossing into the quality editors' lane)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:513px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The three steps are presented in the contract writers' lane and the row associated with writing the blogs. The final step slightly crosses the line, indicating responsibility is being handed off to the quality editors. Consider the rest of the process map, which fits into the quality editor lane.

<img alt="Complete swimlane diagram showing the "Contracted Writers" and "Quality Editors" lanes: Blog written → checked/edited → submitted → Blog post reviewed → "Meets Guidelines?" decision (N returns to editing / Y continues) → Line edit as necessary → Format Post → Schedule post for publication in next" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


You can see that the quality editor's responsibilities actually span the writing and publishing phases. More importantly, you can see that, if the blog doesn't meet the guidelines, the editor sends it back to the writer. The team can see here that there's a possibility of rework in this process, and can see exactly how that rework is handled. The complete process map is shown in the image below.

<img alt="Complete swimlane diagram of the blog-generation process, with all three columns (Marketing Team, Contracted Writers, Quality Editors) and three rows (Idea creation, Blog writing, Blog posting) fully filled in" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:631px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


Although this is a fairly basic example, in terms of process maps, it includes every basic premise of building a swimlane process map. You can apply these fundamentals to build simple to very complex process maps for any process, in Excel or with Word, or any other program that includes process map shapes as an option.

### Tips for Building Concise, Appealing Process Maps

It's true that the process maps shown in the images above are somewhat rough. That was done on purpose, to show how building a process map happens while you're brainstorming and thinking through the process. If the process map's only purpose is to provide visual guidance for a Six Sigma team while it works through the DMAIC process, you can leave the process map in a draft state.

If you plan to use the process map in presentations or training documents, though, consider refining it a bit. First, make sure every color combination you used will work well in whatever medium you plan to use the map in. The map above features white text on a blue background in each shape, which might not work well in documents printed in black and white.

Next, take time to make sure the shapes and arrows are aligned in an aesthetically pleasing and logical way. Review your map to make sure the arrows are pointing the right direction, try to avoid arrows crossing too much, and make sure the start and end of each arrow touch a process shape. This helps reduce confusion when you're not there to explain.

Finally, use concise, active language whenever possible, to keep the text in each shape short and understandable. Here are a few edits that could be made to the example above to make the language more active and concise.

- "Team lists new ideas for next month's blog" becomes "Generate blog ideas"
- "Team chooses 8 to 10 ideas from those brainstormed" becomes "Choose 8 to 10 ideas"
- "Blogs are assigned to writers" becomes "Assign posts to writers"
- "Blog is written" becomes "Write blog"

You can see the shorter versions almost always start with an action verb, which is ideal in process mapping and flowchart creation.
